Siftei Da'at: Since it walked on the ground (Shach). If it didn't walk, it is permitted by the slaughter of its mother rabbinically. If its mother died, and [the fetus] is a nine month fetus that died, it is forbidden rabbinically. If a nine month fetus lives, it is permitted rabbinically through its own slaughter.
Introduction to the Laws of Lung Examina: Prior to elucidating the laws governing lung examination, I wish to offer several preliminary observations, each of which will be discussed in its proper context; we now commence, with God’s help.

Know that with regard to the treifot (disqualifying defects) stated concerning the lung, one must investigate whether all of them fall under the category of perforation, or of conditions that will ultimately lead to perforation, or whether some do not belong to the general classification of perforation at all. This inquiry arises because I have observed that our master, the “Light of Israel,” the eminent gaon and author of Tevu’at Shor, whose words guide us in these laws and are illuminating to the eyes, examined this issue to some extent, and I shall, with God’s help, elaborate upon it. Behold, the Arba'ah Turim opens with the statement that “a lung that has been perforated is treifah,” and proceeds to discuss cases such as substitution (ḥalif) and deficiency; see the Derishah there, which states explicitly that all lung treifot are due to the principle that they will ultimately become perforated, and this is also the consensus of most halakhic authorities. Even a deficiency in the external substance of the lung—where the missing portion is of the size of a bent kaf, which we deem disqualifying—is understood as a lesion that will ultimately result in perforation, as will be explained. However, Maimonides (Rambam) distinguishes among them: in his view, some fall under the category of perforation, while others are classified as deficiencies; for, as you can see in Chapter 10 of Hilkhot Sheḥitah, the Joseph Karo notes that under the category of perforation, Rambam includes cases such as a punctured lung, a perforated bronchial tube, a sealed lung, decay of the bronchial passages, putrid discharge, foul fluids, turbid fluids, liquefaction of the lung tissue, changes in coloration, adhesions, and lobes arranged out of order, whereas under the category of deficiency he includes cases such as a lack in the number of lobes, interchange of lobes or absence of proper division between them, a missing portion of the lung’s substance, partial desiccation, shrinkage due to fear, excess lobes on the dorsal side, and a lung found to be inflated and rigid. This distinction is indeed well-founded, for Rambam, in Chapters 6 and 7, enumerates perforations, while in Chapter 8 he enumerates deficiencies, classifying each accordingly, as noted by the Kesef Mishneh. See also Rashi on Talmud Bavli (s.v. lo tafik), who appears to group the subsequent cases under the categories of perforation or deficiency, while treating substitution as a form of deficiency; prima facie, this suggests agreement with Rambam that substitution is classified as a deficiency, although Rashi’s words may be interpreted differently, yet the straightforward reading supports this view. Further, see the Kesef Mishneh (ad loc., Chapter 8, halakhah 7), who challenges Rashi: if so, why does the Gemara later ask “or if it is lacking—for whom is this taught?” and not answer that substitution is included within deficiency? One might also question why this difficulty does not arise in Rambam’s formulation—why not interpret the case in accordance with all opinions as referring to a deficiency in the lung’s substance? Moreover, according to both Rashi and Rambam, why not establish the case as referring to the absence of a single lobe, which is universally deemed treifah? It may be suggested that, although Rambam in his commentary to the Mishnah appears to interpret “a lung lacking in its number of lobes” in this way, the Gemara is reluctant to adopt such an explanation, since it would follow a fortiori that if perforation renders the lung treifah, then certainly a deficiency would as well, and otherwise it would have needed to enumerate all such cases explicitly; however, this is not a decisive objection, since all such cases may be considered as one category. The case of substitution, however, remains a valid difficulty: why not say that “deficiency” includes substitution? This matter still requires further analysis, as noted elsewhere (see Siman 36). Finally, from Rashi’s words it would seem that if there are three lobes on the right and four on the left, the lung is kosher, for otherwise the Mishnah should have counted more than eighteen cases, since this would not constitute a deficiency; and if one argues that an extra lobe is included under deficiency, we do not rule in accordance with Rava that an additional lobe arranged in order is permissible. One may answer that this applies only where such an arrangement is typical—namely, when the left does not exceed the right—but where the left side has more lobes than the right, this is atypical, and we therefore classify it under the principle that an excess is akin to a deficiency, a point that will be clarified further below
Introduction to Siman 39: I shall begin with that which we concluded. It is established (קיי״ל) in Talmud Bavli, Chullin 12a that we follow the majority (אזלינן בתר רובא). Rashi (s.v. “Pesach”) explains that this principle is either a הלכה למשה מסיני (a law transmitted to Moses at Sinai) or derived from the verse “אחרי רבים להטות” (“to incline after the majority”), with no distinction between a majority that is present before us (איתא קמן) and one that is not (ליתא קמן); accordingly, we rely upon this principle and do not investigate the eighteen טריפות (fatal defects), including perforations of the lung where irregularities are common, such that if no inspection was performed the animal remains kosher, relying on Rav Huna, and this ruling is not publicized—hence it is established that we do not examine for the eighteen טריפות. This, however, requires analysis: why is this so, given that wherever clarification is possible we generally undertake it, as is evident at the beginning of Talmud Bavli, Pesachim and from the principle that “most who are found [in a given category]…,” which implies that, where feasible, verification should be carried out? One might suggest that here there is both a majority and a presumption (חזקה) that the animal survives twelve months, which would suffice where it indeed lived twelve months; yet a presumption not empirically verified is of no legal consequence (cf. Tosafot to Chullin 11a, s.v. “אתי”). Furthermore, with respect to a perforation of the esophagus or a severance of the trachea at the place of slaughter, why do we not examine—should we not combine the minority possibility (מיעוטא) with the presumption, yielding an even balance (פלגא) at least on a rabbinic level? As for the slaughter itself, one might argue that perhaps the cut occurred at the site of a preexisting perforation and that the Sages did not impose stringency; nevertheless, why is no examination conducted at all? If one were to argue that this is a case of an exceedingly rare minority (מיעוטא דמיעוטא), such that the usual rule of combining factors does not apply (cf. Talmud Bavli, Yevamot 119a and many similar passages, as noted by Maharsha), and that such combination is only rabbinic, one could further suggest that this is a non-prevalent minority (מיעוטא דלא שכיח), which would resolve the difficulty; however, if so, how does the Talmud in Chullin derive the general rule of following the majority from cases such as the עולה (burnt offering), the עגלה (heifer), and similar derivations, which may be distinguished as involving a non-prevalent minority conceded even by Rabbi Meir? At first glance, the Maharsha appears to offer his second answer in accordance with Rabbi Meir, whereas for the Rabbis the first answer suffices, yet this is strained, as it implies a dispute about empirical reality; moreover, what can be said regarding the inspection of the lung, where the minority is in fact common and prevalent—would we maintain that even there, according to Rabbi Meir, it is deemed non-prevalent? This remains problematic. The more cogent resolution is that proposed by Minchat Yaakov (klal 59, §8), that wherever verification entails significant effort (טירחא) one is not required to clarify, even where a presumption exists, whereas where no such effort is involved, clarification is required even in cases governed by a majority—and likewise in cases of double doubt (ספק ספקא), which is analogous to a majority; accordingly, inspection for the eighteen טריפות constitutes a considerable burden, and we therefore rely on the majority. As for why we do not examine the esophagus or trachea, the rule of combining factors on a rabbinic level applies only where the ספק arises independently, but not in these instances, and this is not comparable to Talmud Bavli, Yevamot 139, where the minority does not arise through an action (see Tosafot ad loc.), and see also the Maharsha to Talmud Bavli, Bekhorot 2a (s.v. “חלב”), which requires further consideration; I have discussed this at length in my responsa Ginat Veradim, and see also Orach Chaim, Hilchot Pesach, siman 432 with the commentaries of the Magen Avraham and Pri Chadash, and, God willing, I will elaborate more fully elsewhere.

The examination of the lung is, in fact, mentioned in Talmud Bavli, Beitzah 25b, where it is stated that “planting cuts off the feet of the enemies of Israel”; some commentators explain this as referring to the lung, and that, due to financial loss, permission was granted there to proceed without inspection—see the Rosh ad loc., and see also the Rashba to Talmud Bavli, Chullin 9a, who writes similarly and brings proof from the Yerushalmi, stating that there is reason to suspect that perhaps the lung was perforated, while the presumption is that the internal organs are sound, implying that when the matter is present before us (איתא קמן), an inspection is required; he further adduces proof from the Yerushalmi (Beitzah ch. 4), where it is stated that inspection of the lung is rabbinic and separation of demai is rabbinic, and just as one inspects a טריפה on a festival, so too one separates demai on a festival, in a case where no defect had arisen, for otherwise it would constitute a prohibited new development, and he also cites Midrash Yelamdenu, “Rabbi Yora ben Pediyah said: who will uncover the dust from your eyes, Adam the First, for a person slaughters an animal and inspects the lung”; however, regarding other טריפות, even when the matter is present before us, one need not inspect, and proof is brought from the statement that perhaps where it is not possible it is different, implying that according to the Rabbis even where it is possible inspection is not required, and similarly later (Chullin 51a) it is stated that if an animal fell it requires inspection, and (47a) that in the case of a sealed lung one brings a knife to test whether it bubbles, and likewise regarding a lung that produces a sound, implying that where no defect is apparent no inspection is required, and they further state explicitly (51a) regarding a case where a hind leg was trailing that such a condition is common, all the more so where no defect has arisen at all; yet I, a lowly servant who bows from afar before the dust of the sanctuary of his holy words, find that these arguments require considerable analysis and precision, for as to the first proof—that even where inspection is possible the Rabbis do not require it—it may be said that this applies specifically to a minor, where we do not delay until maturity, but with respect to examining the eighteen טריפות, which can be clarified immediately, it is possible that we do investigate, and regarding the second proof, “if it fell it requires inspection,” one may interpret that if one did not inspect even post facto it is prohibited, or that inspection is required to determine whether the form of the organ has been compromised, in which case even if it remains whole it is forbidden, as explained later (siman 58) in the laws of a fallen animal, and indeed the Rashba in Torat HaBayit agrees with the Rambam that inspection there is also for crushing injuries, so no proof may be derived, and as for the third proof from a sealed lung, it may be understood that every lung must be tested by inflation to see whether it emits air, but a sealed lung cannot be tested in this way and therefore requires cutting, and although one might object that cutting is ineffective since the membrane could simply be torn and perhaps the perforation occurred at the place of the cut, nevertheless the formulation that where no defect is present we do not inspect does not fully accord with this explanation, and moreover it may still be argued that where inspection is not possible it is different, whereas where it is possible one must clarify as much as one can, and the fourth proof from a lung that produces a sound is indeed strong, since when the location is known one applies saliva only at that place, although ordinarily one must inspect the entire lung due to concern for perforations, yet even this is not entirely clear, for according to Rashi the inspection is due to adhesions rather than perforations, and although adhesions do not occur without perforations, later authorities have written that perforations without adhesions are uncommon since a scab quickly forms, so where no adhesion is seen we do not suspect perforations, and even if one argues that this reduces the concern from a prevalent minority it remains at least a minority, in which case the entire lung should still be examined, unless one maintains that it is only an exceedingly rare minority and therefore no inspection is required, and one may answer that the Rashba, consistent with his view, demonstrated in Torat HaBayit that the law does not follow Rashi, yet a difficulty remains that perhaps for perforations simple inflation suffices while for a sounding lung saliva is required and where the location is unknown the entire lung must be tested, and the fifth proof from the case where no inspection was performed because such a condition is common may be interpreted as referring only to changes in the form of the organ attributable to a fall, yet this is untenable, for it is said there that perhaps the spinal cord was severed and they inspected and found that it was so, indicating that the dispute concerns whether inspection for the eighteen טריפות is required at all, which is indeed compelling evidence; nevertheless, I have not fully understood the earlier proofs, and therefore it appears that no definitive proof can be derived from them, for statements that there is no concern of crushing refer specifically to changes in form, and likewise cases such as a perforated lung manipulated by hand or the rule that we do not compare blisters yield no proof, and thus one may maintain that ab initio wherever clarification is possible we do clarify, but if one did not inspect immediately and the perforation may be attributed to post-slaughter handling by the butcher we do not perform comparative tests to demonstrate this, since such conditions may change, and where verification is not feasible we rely on the majority and the presumption, attributing the perforation to post-slaughter causes, while nevertheless remaining obligated to examine manually wherever possible in order to detect any טריפה and thereby avoid prohibition.
